title:
Comment of Shaun Haskins in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15424-000
Submission Date: 10/19/2026

documents.name: 151649.txt
documents.text:
Shaun Haskins, Machias, ME.
To the Secretary:
We are writing on behalf of Living Tide, a multi-national alliance of  tribal and non-tribal individuals, most of whom live in and around the Passamaquoddy Bay Region, including from the city of Eastport and the adjacent Peskotomuhkati (Passamaquoddy) communities of Sipayik and Skutik (in what are now known as Maine and southwestern New Brunswick, respectively). We are business leaders, activists, civic leaders, community organizers, and scientists committed to the ecological and social health and well-being of our home region and one Earth.  We are united in opposition to the request filed for the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub. We are deeply concerned about the negative impacts this project will have on our community, our environment, our local economy, and future generations.
--
As online maps show, there are AI data centers erupting across the US and Canada, including areas that are facing drought conditions. We are deeply troubled by the potential environmental, cultural, social, and economic impacts associated with a development of this size, cumulative impacts of other similar projects, and significant energy and water requirements.
Our concerns extend beyond the immediate project site. The potential effects on the Bay of Fundy, marine ecosystems, wildlife, fisheries, regional energy supply, and surrounding communities must be fully understood before this project is allowed to proceed.
--
For the Peskotomuhkati peoples, protection of the land and water is inseparable from the protection of our culture, rights, traditional practices, and responsibilities to future generations. Meaningful consultation must therefore occur before irreversible decisions are made and must include consideration of Indigenous Knowledge and the potential impacts individual and community health and well-being including as they relate to Aboriginal and Treaty rights. The region where the proposed project is located is within Peskotumuhkati Territory and elected Tribal Representative of the Passamaquoddy Tribe to the State of Maine Aaron Dana explains:

 “Passamaquoddy Bay is not simply a body of water to our people. It holds deep cultural, historical, and spiritual significance. Our connection to these waters has existed since time immemorial, and our responsibility and passion to protect them remains unwavering.
We will not stand by while developments that may impact our ancestral lands and waters move forward without our consent or careful consideration. Our duty is to safeguard our territory, our natural resources, and our way of life for future generations.”
Any changes to water temperature, water quality, underwater soundscape, fish habitat, migration patterns, or marine productivity will affect commercial fisheries as well as Food, Social and Ceremonial (FSC) fisheries and traditional harvesting. These fisheries support livelihoods, food security, culture, and the exercise of Indigenous rights as outlined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, particularly Article 8b and Article 26-1.
Effects within the Bay will directly impact Peskotomuhkati kin (marine wildlife). 
--
Climate change is causing drastic changes, including shifts to weather patterns and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). The Gulf of Maine and Bay of Fundy are warming at an accelerated rate - more quickly than other parts of the world. Changes have already been felt, including changes in abundance and health of plankton following a marine heatwave in 2012 - which led to changes in the critically endangered North Atlantic Right Whale migration patterns as they attempt to find food. 

The DeepGreen projects would increase local ocean temperatures considerably, and we do not understand the potentially devastating cumulative effects this may have, given the fact that the Bay is already experiencing drastic warming. Species loss and species migration are predicted - but there are many nuances (is there ample food for migrating species, are there predators, will the ecosystem rebalance in a short time), and it will be important to study the long-term impacts to native species, habitats, and coastal livelihoods.
--
‘DeepGreen’ proposes a 27.1 acres in Western Passage near Eastport, which is feeding habitat for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales, minke whales, fin whales, humpback whales, leatherback sea turtles and other marine animals. Increased vessel traffic for even baseline studies will create extra noise and possibilities for collision, and increased underwater noise, impacting echolocation for cetaceans. The Bay is critical habitat for seabirds, migratory birds, sea-run fish, many benthic species, delicate sponges, anemones, crustaceans including lobster; sea stars, urchins, sea cucumbers, to name a few. 

Western Passage is part of important migratory routes for a wide range of species including alewife, sturgeon and other sea-run fish, as well as marine species including Atlantic herring.   Large, loud, warm infrastructure like tidal turbines and an AI data centre have a high probability of disrupting migration, though with limited information available on the proposal, we can not fully assess the risk. Given the ongoing restoration efforts on the Skutik River, it is particularly important to limit impacts on the migratory routes of species returning to the Skutik watershed.

The data center cannot be considered in isolation from the transmission lines, pipelines, generating facilities, roads, land clearing, infilling, underwater blasting, and other infrastructure required to support it. The combined footprint will affect forests, wetlands, waterways, wildlife corridors, fish habitat, species at risk, and areas traditionally and presently used by Indigenous peoples. 

Noise, light, and thermal pollution and increased water temperatures associated with cooling and industrial operations must be carefully examined in assessments. Even small changes in water temperature can affect sensitive marine habitats, fish migration, spawning, food sources, and the broader marine ecosystem. Effects of noise and light pollution on many marine creatures and migratory birds are well documented. The cumulative effects on the Bay must be considered.
--
AI data centers require enormous and continuous amounts of electricity. At a time when Maine is already facing significant future electricity demands, FERC must clearly explain where the power for this project will come from and whether supplying such a large industrial user could affect electricity availability, reliability, future rates, and energy security for Maine residents and businesses.

We are concerned that the extraordinary electricity demands associated with this and other AI data centers could result in increased natural-gas consumption, additional fossil-fuel infrastructure, or pressure for expanded nuclear power generation. The environmental impacts, greenhouse-gas emissions, nuclear waste, long-term liabilities, and risks associated with supplying this amount of energy must be included when assessing the true impact of the project.
--
Eastport, Skutik, and Sipayik are active working waterfronts where fishers, rockweed harvesters, and eco-tourism rely on healthy marine ecosystems. Downeast Maine has a long history, reliance, and close relationship with the ocean. Countless generations of Wabanaki and settler families have been able to survive and thrive thanks to the bounty of this incredibly rich and diverse coastal ecosystem. The rich upwellings of nutrients mixing in the currents and high tides in the mouth of the Bay of Fundy make this place, historically, incredibly biodiverse and abundant. Basque fishermen described coming to the banks of eastern North America in the 1500s, and the shoals of fish were so thick that their wooden ships were slowed to a halt. Much of this abundance has been lost due to overharvesting, damming, causeways, and heavy industrialization and pollution. We are only just beginning to reverse this damage. Alewife populations have gone from a meager 900 fish in 2002 to well over a million in 2025. When given a chance, nature can thrive once more. 

Lobster are sensitive to increased water temperatures, and the Bay of Fundy and Gulf of Maine already experience climate change-linked temperature increases. A further increase in water temperature would compound existing environmental issues, and could lead to added economic stress for fishing local communities.

Living Tide knows this place is special - and adding an underwater AI data center would put present and future coastal livelihoods at unnecessary risk. 

The protection of our waters, fisheries, wildlife, communities, and future generations must remain top priority when determining whether and and under what conditions this development should proceed. These impacts must also be considered cumulatively. Looking at individual components separately does not provide an accurate picture of what a development of this magnitude could mean for the land, water, Bay of Fundy, fisheries, wildlife, energy system, and communities over the long term.   
   
We respectfully ask that the Peskotomuhkati Nation are meaningfully involved throughout that process. If they are, we believe For the reasons listed above, you must reject thisthe project is in the public interest.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and Thank you for your time, consideration, and dedication to reviewing the concerns of the affected public.
Sincerely,
 
Living Tide Members:
